Unit 2 — Learning: Paradigms, Regression and the First Classifier

This notebook is the R edition of the second unit of the course. The lecture slides are a map; this text is the territory. Unit 1 ended with a classifier “trained” by computing two means; this unit asks what training means in general — what it is for a machine to learn — and answers as a definition (Section 1), as a step in the practice of data science (Section 2), as a family of paradigms (Sections 3–5) and as an algorithm you can run by hand (Sections 6–7). The official plan omits regression, the simplest learning problem and the one in which model, loss, optimisation and overfitting can be seen without distraction; regression is therefore the core of this unit, and logistic regression — a regression model used as a classifier — is the first classifier studied properly. Every figure and number in the text is produced by the R code you can see and change.

Learning objectives

  • State Mitchell’s definition of learning, identify task, performance and experience in a clinical problem, and distinguish inductive from deductive inference.
  • Define data science, structured and unstructured data and the seven steps of a project, and locate machine learning within them.
  • Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, semi- and self-supervised learning with a biomedical example of each; use “class”, “label” and “target” correctly.
  • Define a classifier and its decision boundary, and relate the statistical, neural and evolutionary approaches to Unit 1.
  • Derive and solve the normal equations, interpret coefficients, \(R^2\) and residuals; implement gradient descent and explain the learning rate; recognise overfitting and explain ridge.
  • Explain the sigmoid, log-loss and threshold of logistic regression, compute one probability by hand, and extend to several classes.
  • Say what k-means and value iteration learn, and from what.

How to read this notebook

Read linearly once, executing each code chunk and reading the paragraph that interprets it; then return by section. Green boxes are exercises that change one thing in the chunk above; blue boxes key ideas; orange boxes misconceptions; purple boxes links to other units or to BGM324. Only base R and the packages MASS, class, e1071, rpart, rpart.plot, nnet, cluster, mlbench and ggplot2 are used; in a fresh Google Colab R runtime run once install.packages(c(“e1071”,“rpart.plot”,“nnet”,“cluster”,“mlbench”)). The datasets ship with mlbench or with base R, so nothing is downloaded. Supplement S0 covers the R toolkit, Supplement S1 the evaluation methodology previewed in Section 11. 

# Setup: packages used throughout, and a fixed seed so every quoted number is reproducible.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(MASS); library(class); library(e1071); library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)
  library(nnet); library(cluster); library(mlbench); library(ggplot2)
})
set.seed(0)
BLUE <- "#2b5d9b"; ORANGE <- "#d2691e"; GREEN <- "#3a7d44"; GREY <- "#8a8a8a"
options(digits = 5)
R.version.string
## [1] "R version 4.5.3 (2026-03-11)"

The printout is the R version these notes were knitted with. R is a language built for data — statistics, modelling and graphics are in the language rather than bolted on[36] — and it is the language the official laboratory plan uses, so these notebooks double as lab material; the R companion to the whole course is An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R.[39]

1. What it means to learn

1.1 Mitchell’s definition

The field’s operational definition of learning is Tom Mitchell’s:[1]

Definition (Mitchell, 1997)

A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.

It is purely behavioural, and it turns “does the system learn?” into three concrete questions every application paper should answer.

Component Question Breast-cancer example (Unit 1) Hospital-ward example
Task T What is the system to do? Assign malignant or benign to an aspirate described by nuclear features Predict whether a patient will deteriorate within 24 h
Performance P How is doing well measured? Agreement with the biopsy (better: the two error rates separately) Sensitivity at a fixed false-alarm rate
Experience E What data does it see? 683 labelled aspirates from Wisconsin Vital signs and outcomes of past admissions

The idea predates the definition. In 1959 Arthur Samuel’s checkers program improved by playing against itself and adjusting the weights of its evaluation function; he called it “machine learning”: programming computers to learn from experience so as to eliminate much of the detailed programming.[2] The shift from expert systems to learned systems (Unit 1) is the shift from writing the rule to writing the procedure that finds the rule.

1.2 The three ingredients of a learning algorithm

Every learning algorithm in this course is built from three parts:

  1. A model (hypothesis space): a family of functions \(f_\theta\) indexed by parameters \(\theta\) — intercept and slope for a line, millions of weights for a network; the algorithm can only find a member of the family.
  2. A loss function \(L(\theta)\): how badly \(f_\theta\) performs on the training data — squared errors, misclassifications, negative log-probability of the labels; it operationalises Mitchell’s \(P\).
  3. An optimiser: the search for the parameters minimising the loss — a closed formula (Section 6), iterative descent (Section 7) or evolutionary search (Section 4, Unit 7).

Domingos compresses this into learning = representation + evaluation + optimisation; his dozen further lessons — generalisation is what counts, data alone are not enough, overfitting has many faces — this unit illustrates one by one.[3]

Common misconception

“Training” is not “programming the answer”. The human supplies the form (model), the criterion (loss), the data and the labels; the algorithm finds the parameters. When a model “was trained on 100,000 X-rays”, nobody wrote the rule that reads the X-ray, and nobody may be able to read it.

1.3 Inductive and deductive inference

Learning in Mitchell’s sense is inductive inference: from particular observations to a general rule. Deductive inference goes the other way, and the two differ in every respect that matters:

Deductive Inductive
Direction general → specific: rules to cases specific → general: cases to a rule
Role apply knowledge someone already has discover knowledge from data
Guarantee conclusion certain if the premises are true conclusion probable, never certain
Risk rigidity: fails on cases the rules did not anticipate over-generalisation: a rule that fits the sample, not the world
In AI expert systems, logic (Unit 1, Section 3.1) machine learning (this course)

“All mammals have lungs; a whale is a mammal; therefore a whale has lungs” is deduction: certain, contained in the premises. “Every mammal examined so far has lungs; therefore all mammals have lungs” is induction: how the rule was obtained, fallible in principle and reliable in practice. Rats learn inductively: one that falls ill after a novel bait avoids that bait — and that flavour — thereafter, which is why poisoned baits fail against rats so quickly. A spam filter shows both in software. A deductive filter stores every message marked as spam and blocks exact copies: it never makes a false accusation and is defeated by one changed character. An inductive filter learns which words characterise the marked messages and scores new ones by them: it generalises to messages never seen, and is sometimes wrong. Memorisation is deduction from a table; learning is induction to a rule, and the methodology of this course exists because induction is fallible and its reliability must be measured.

2. From data science to machine learning

2.1 What data science is

Data science extracts knowledge and actionable conclusions from data by combining statistics, computing and domain knowledge; its roots are in statistics, and Donoho’s historical account asks what is genuinely new in it.[4] Machine learning is the part of data science that builds models which learn from data; data science also includes everything before (asking the question; collecting, cleaning and exploring the data) and after (interpreting and communicating). It follows the scientific method — observe, question, collect data designed to answer it, analyse, conclude, communicate so others can check — at a scale classical experimentation did not face. In a real project model fitting takes a small fraction of the time; the rest goes to the data.

2.2 Kinds of data and where they come from

Structured data conform to a predefined data model — a table with fixed columns and types, as the data matrix of Unit 1 — and live in relational databases queried with SQL and, institutionally, in a data warehouse, a curated store built for known analyses. Unstructured data have no predefined model — clinical notes, images, audio, sequences — and live as files or in NoSQL databases and, at scale, in a data lake of raw data interpreted only when read. Most hospital data are unstructured, and the pattern-recognition pipeline of Unit 1 is the machinery that turns them into the structured table every method here requires. Quantitative data admit arithmetic; qualitative data are categories, text or judgements. Analysis methods are named by their product: classification (a category), regression (a number), clustering (groups without labels) and data mining, the discovery of patterns such as association rules (Section 3.3).

Data come from transactional systems (hospital, pharmacy, laboratory records), public sources (statistics, repositories such as UCI), experiments and trials, curated databases (ChEMBL, DrugBank, UniProt), the literature and patents, sensors (monitors, wearables, imaging) and media. Each carries its own biases.

2.3 Purposes

Projects describe a phenomenon (how many patients were readmitted), explain it (which factors are associated), predict it (which patients will be readmitted) and, downstream, reduce cost, mitigate risk and improve efficiency. Machine learning serves mainly prediction.

2.4 The seven steps of a data-science project

  1. Problem identification. The question, the unit of analysis, the target, the measure of success, the decision informed — Mitchell’s \(T\), \(P\), \(E\).
  2. Data collection. From the sources above, with a legal basis and documented provenance.
  3. Data cleaning. Quantify missing data and decide (discard, impute, model); detect outliers and judge them; remove unwanted records and columns; unify structure and format.
  4. Exploratory data analysis (EDA). Descriptive statistics, univariate and multivariate (correlations, cross-tabulations); hypothesis tests where warranted; above all graphical representation.
  5. Feature engineering. Attribute selection; class balance; grouping of categories; normalisation (Section 7 shows why); feature correlations, since correlated features destabilise linear models (Section 6.5).
  6. Machine-learning prediction. Choose, fit, evaluate honestly (Section 11, Supplement S1), iterate back to steps 3–5.
  7. Data storytelling. Communicate figures, uncertainty and limitations to the people who will act, in their language.

Three chunks illustrate steps 3–5 on the Wisconsin breast-cancer data,[5] shipped by the mlbench package[37] and loaded here for the whole notebook. The shipped version has 683 complete aspirates described by nine nuclear-shape features scored 1–10 and labelled benign or malignant; since those data are clean, the first chunk deletes 5 % of the values at random to illustrate missingness.

# Step 3, data cleaning: curate the data, inject missingness for illustration, flag outliers by z-score.
data(BreastCancer, package = "mlbench")
bc <- BreastCancer[, -1]                                  # drop the Id column
bc <- bc[complete.cases(bc), ]                            # drop the 16 incomplete records
bc[, 1:9] <- lapply(bc[, 1:9], function(z) as.numeric(as.character(z)))  # ordinal -> numeric
y <- ifelse(bc$Class == "benign", 1L, 0L)                 # y: 1 = benign, 0 = malignant (as in Unit 1)
X <- bc[, 1:9]

set.seed(0); miss <- matrix(runif(nrow(X) * 9) < 0.05, nrow(X))   # delete 5% of cells at random
cat(sprintf("cells missing: %.1f%% | rows with >=1 missing: %.1f%% | rows surviving 'drop any NA row': %d of %d\n",
            100*mean(miss), 100*mean(rowSums(miss) > 0), sum(rowSums(miss) == 0), nrow(X)))
## cells missing: 5.4% | rows with >=1 missing: 40.3% | rows surviving 'drop any NA row': 408 of 683
z <- scale(X)                                             # z-scores of the clean data
cat(sprintf("values beyond 4 SD: %d in %d patients; most extreme feature '%s' at z = %.1f\n",
            sum(abs(z) > 4), sum(rowSums(abs(z) > 4) > 0),
            names(which.max(apply(abs(z), 2, max))), max(abs(z))))
## values beyond 4 SD: 14 in 14 patients; most extreme feature 'Mitoses' at z = 4.8

With 5 % of cells missing at random, about 40 % of rows have a gap and dropping incomplete rows would keep 408 patients of 683 — which is why imputation is normal practice and missingness is quantified per column. The z-score screen flags 14 values beyond four standard deviations in 14 patients; whether they are errors or extreme tumours is for the pathologist to judge.

# Step 4, exploratory data analysis: class means and the correlation structure of the nine features.
means <- t(sapply(X, function(z) tapply(z, bc$Class, mean)))
ratio <- sort(means[, "malignant"] / means[, "benign"], decreasing = TRUE)
cat("features whose malignant mean is the largest multiple of the benign mean:\n")
## features whose malignant mean is the largest multiple of the benign mean:
print(round(ratio[1:4], 2))
##     Bare.nuclei       Cell.size Normal.nucleoli      Cell.shape 
##            5.66            5.04            4.64            4.64
corr <- cor(X)
dfp <- data.frame(f1 = rep(colnames(X), 9), f2 = rep(colnames(X), each = 9), r = as.vector(corr))
ggplot(dfp, aes(f1, f2, fill = r)) + geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), size = 2.6,
            colour = ifelse(abs(dfp$r) > 0.6, "white", "black")) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = BLUE, mid = "white", high = ORANGE, midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Pearson correlation between the nine nuclear features", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1))

Figure 1. Pearson correlation between the nine nuclear features, drawn with ggplot2.[40] Cell size and cell shape correlate at 0.91 — two measures of the same nuclear enlargement — so a model given both receives that information twice (Section 6.5 shows the consequence). The table shows that bare nuclei, cell size and normal nucleoli differ most between classes (malignant means about five times the benign means), which is why the two features used from Unit 1 onward are clump thickness and cell size. 

# Step 5, feature engineering: class balance, standardisation, and removing redundant features.
cat(sprintf("class balance: %d malignant (%.1f%%), %d benign (%.1f%%)\n",
            sum(y == 0), 100*mean(y == 0), sum(y == 1), 100*mean(y == 1)))
## class balance: 239 malignant (35.0%), 444 benign (65.0%)
scaled <- scale(X)
summ <- data.frame(raw_mean = colMeans(X), raw_sd = apply(X, 2, sd),
                   scaled_mean = round(colMeans(scaled), 10), scaled_sd = apply(scaled, 2, sd))
print(round(summ[c("Cl.thickness", "Cell.size", "Bare.nuclei", "Mitoses"), ], 3))
##              raw_mean raw_sd scaled_mean scaled_sd
## Cl.thickness    4.442  2.821           0         1
## Cell.size       3.151  3.065           0         1
## Bare.nuclei     3.545  3.644           0         1
## Mitoses         1.603  1.733           0         1
fc <- abs(cor(X)); drop <- character(0)                   # drop one of every pair with |r| > 0.9
for (i in 1:8) for (j in (i+1):9)
  if (fc[i, j] > 0.9 && !(colnames(X)[i] %in% drop)) drop <- union(drop, colnames(X)[j])
cat("features dropped as redundant (|r| > 0.9 with a kept feature):", length(drop), "->", drop, "\n")
## features dropped as redundant (|r| > 0.9 with a kept feature): 1 -> Cell.shape

The classes are 35 % malignant and 65 % benign: mild enough to need no correction, but a classifier that always says “benign” is already 65 % accurate, the baseline every reported accuracy must beat. Standardisation gives every feature mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so that features scored on the same 1–10 scale but with different spreads enter distance- and gradient-based methods equally. The redundancy screen drops one feature, cell shape, as nearly a copy of cell size. None of this is “machine learning”, and all of it affects the result more than the choice among the classifiers of Section 5.

Data science versus machine learning

Machine learning is step 6 of seven. A project excellent at step 6 and careless at steps 1, 3 or 7 answers the wrong question, learns the artefacts of its data, or is never used. The methods of this course are necessary, not sufficient.

3. The paradigms of learning

The paradigms differ in the kind of feedback contained in the experience \(E\), not in the algorithm.

# Schematic of the three classical learning paradigms (conceptual figure).
set.seed(0)
cen <- rbind(c(-1.5, 0), c(1.5, 0.5))
Xb <- rbind(cbind(rnorm(30, cen[1,1], .8), rnorm(30, cen[1,2], .8)),
            cbind(rnorm(30, cen[2,1], .8), rnorm(30, cen[2,2], .8)))
yb <- rep(0:1, each = 30)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
# supervised
plot(Xb, col = ifelse(yb == 0, BLUE, ORANGE), pch = 19, cex = .7, xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "feature 1", ylab = "feature 2", main = "Supervised: inputs + labels")
abline(a = 0.2, b = 8, lty = 2); legend("bottomleft", c("class 0", "class 1", "boundary"),
     col = c(BLUE, ORANGE, "black"), pch = c(19, 19, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 2), bty = "n", cex = .8)
# unsupervised
plot(Xb, col = GREY, pch = 19, cex = .7, xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "feature 1", ylab = "feature 2", main = "Unsupervised: inputs only")
text(0, 2.6, "find structure: groups, directions, outliers", cex = .8, font = 3)
# reinforcement
plot(0:10, 0:10, type = "n", axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Reinforcement: actions + rewards")
rect(1, 6.2, 9, 8.8, col = adjustcolor(BLUE, .2), border = NA); text(5, 7.5, "Agent (policy)")
rect(1, 1.2, 9, 3.8, col = adjustcolor(ORANGE, .2), border = NA); text(5, 2.5, "Environment\n(patient, game, robot)")
arrows(7.5, 6.1, 7.5, 3.9, length = .12); text(8.3, 5, "action", cex = .8)
arrows(2.5, 3.9, 2.5, 6.1, length = .12); text(1.6, 5, "state,\nreward", cex = .8)

par(op)

Figure 2. Left: supervised — every input comes with the correct output and the learner fits a function between them. Centre: unsupervised — the same inputs without labels; two groups are visible, and k-means (Section 10) will find them. Right: reinforcement — no dataset at the outset; an agent acts, observes the new state and a scalar reward, and discovers by trial and error which actions lead to high cumulative reward.

3.1 Supervised learning

The experience is pairs \((\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\): input and correct output, supplied by a “supervisor” — a pathologist, a laboratory, a follow-up visit. The task is a function with \(f(\mathbf{x}) \approx y\) on unseen inputs. A categorical \(y\) makes it classification; a numerical \(y\) (progression, glucose, survival time) makes it regression. They share everything but the loss and the output, so Sections 6–8 do regression and Section 9 turns the machinery into a classifier. Labels encode exactly what we want predicted, which is why most practical impact is supervised; their cost — a radiologist’s time, a biopsy, a year of follow-up — is the paradigm’s limit.

Terminology: class, label, target

In classification class and label are synonyms for the category predicted; target covers both. In regression the target is a continuous value and should not be called a class — there are no classes in a regression problem, and the slides’ use of “class” for the regression output is a slip. Say target or response for regression, class or label for classification.

3.2 Two examples from chemistry

Two problems from computational drug discovery — the research field of the laboratory that prepared this material, and the subject of the QSAR unit of BGM324 — show both forms. The instances are molecules and the features are descriptors computed from the structure: molecular weight (MW), hydrogen-bond donors (HBD) and acceptors (HBA), and polar surface area (PSA) — the descriptors of Lipinski’s “rule of five” for oral absorption (MW < 500, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10; PSA < 140 Å² in later refinements).[6]

Classification: is the molecule an approved drug? A binary label — FDA-approved or not — assembled from fda.gov, DrugBank[7] and the Drug Repurposing Hub (clue.io); given the descriptors of a new molecule, predict it.

Regression: how potent is it? The IC50 of a compound against a target is the concentration at which it inhibits the target’s activity by 50 %; the lower, the more potent, so compound A with IC50 = 10 µM is a better inhibitor than compound B with 1000 µM. Measured values for millions of compound–target pairs are curated in ChEMBL[8] and BindingDB. Because IC50 spans orders of magnitude, the usual target is pIC50 = −log10(IC50 in mol/L): 10 µM is 5, 1 µM is 6, one unit is tenfold in potency, and the errors become closer to Gaussian.

The chunk reproduces both tables with illustrative values (right ranges, not measured compounds). Each follows the workflow of every supervised method: a training step, in which molecules with known labels or pIC50 are given to the algorithm, which adjusts a model’s parameters to reproduce them; and a prediction step, in which the descriptors of a new molecule are fed to the fitted model, which outputs a predicted label or pIC50.

# The two chemistry examples as data frames (illustrative values, not measured data).
drugs <- data.frame(
  MW = c(180.2, 454.6, 285.3, 812.9, 374.4, 1203.3), HBD = c(1, 2, 1, 7, 3, 12),
  HBA = c(3, 6, 4, 13, 5, 19), PSA = c(63.6, 98.1, 46.5, 212.0, 87.3, 345.9),
  FDA_approved = c("yes", "yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "no"),          # the LABEL (class)
  row.names = c("mol_01","mol_02","mol_03","mol_04","mol_05","mol_06"))
potency <- data.frame(
  MW = c(312.4, 298.3, 401.5, 356.8, 275.3), HBD = c(2, 1, 3, 2, 1),
  HBA = c(4, 3, 6, 5, 3), PSA = c(78.2, 55.1, 110.4, 92.0, 48.7),
  IC50_uM = c(10.0, 1000.0, 0.25, 3.2, 150.0),                       # the TARGET (continuous)
  row.names = c("cpd_A","cpd_B","cpd_C","cpd_D","cpd_E"))
potency$pIC50 <- round(-log10(potency$IC50_uM * 1e-6), 2)
cat("CLASSIFICATION: instances x features + a categorical label\n"); print(drugs)
## CLASSIFICATION: instances x features + a categorical label
##            MW HBD HBA   PSA FDA_approved
## mol_01  180.2   1   3  63.6          yes
## mol_02  454.6   2   6  98.1          yes
## mol_03  285.3   1   4  46.5          yes
## mol_04  812.9   7  13 212.0           no
## mol_05  374.4   3   5  87.3          yes
## mol_06 1203.3  12  19 345.9           no
cat("\nREGRESSION: instances x features + a continuous target (pIC50 = -log10 IC50 in mol/L)\n"); print(potency)
## 
## REGRESSION: instances x features + a continuous target (pIC50 = -log10 IC50 in mol/L)
##          MW HBD HBA   PSA IC50_uM pIC50
## cpd_A 312.4   2   4  78.2   10.00  5.00
## cpd_B 298.3   1   3  55.1 1000.00  3.00
## cpd_C 401.5   3   6 110.4    0.25  6.60
## cpd_D 356.8   2   5  92.0    3.20  5.49
## cpd_E 275.3   1   3  48.7  150.00  3.82

Both tables have the shape of the breast-cancer and housing data used below: rows are instances, the last column is what the model must learn — a category in the first, a number in the second. Compound A (pIC50 = 5) beats B (pIC50 = 3) by two orders of magnitude. Real QSAR models use hundreds of descriptors — the situation (\(p\) comparable to \(n\)) in which the regularisation of Section 8 becomes unavoidable.

3.3 Unsupervised learning

The experience is the inputs alone, \(\{\mathbf{x}_i\}\). With no correct answer to approximate, the task is reformulated as finding structure, and the slides name four sub-types, each a part of Unit 5. Clustering groups instances by similarity (Figure 2, centre; Section 10.1). Dimensionality reduction replaces the \(p\) features by a few new ones that retain most of the variation — principal components, or the two-dimensional embeddings used for single-cell data. Feature selection keeps a subset of the original features; its motivation is the curse of dimensionality: at fixed sample size, adding features first helps a classifier and then hurts it, because the data become sparse in a space of growing volume and the model fits noise in irrelevant features — Hughes showed in 1968 that accuracy peaks at an optimal number of features and then declines.[9] How many features help is answered on held-out data (Section 11); the screen of Section 2.4 is the crudest form. Association analysis searches transactional data — purchases, prescriptions, co-occurring diagnoses — for IF–THEN rules (“patients prescribed A and B are also prescribed C”) with sufficient support and confidence; the Apriori algorithm is the classical method,[10] and its rules are the data-mining counterpart of expert-system rules, discovered rather than written. Without labels the performance measure is ambiguous — how good is a clustering? — the paradigm’s central difficulty, and also what makes it cheap.

3.4 Reinforcement learning

The experience is generated by the learner’s actions: an agent observes a state, chooses an action, receives a scalar reward and a new state; the task is a policy — states to actions — maximising cumulative reward. The feedback is evaluative (how good the action was, not what the right one was) and delayed, hence the credit-assignment problem of attributing outcomes to earlier actions. Sutton and Barto’s textbook is the reference.[11] AlphaGo was reinforcement learning; in medicine it has been used, controversially, to propose fluid and vasopressor dosing in sepsis.[12] Section 10.2 implements the two basic algorithms.

3.5 Modern additions: semi-supervised and self-supervised learning

Semi-supervised learning uses a small labelled set with a large unlabelled one: the unlabelled data cannot name the classes, but a boundary through a sparse region is more plausible than one cutting a dense cluster.[13] Self-supervised learning manufactures labels from the data — hide part of an input (the next word, a masked image patch) and predict it — then fine-tunes the learned representation on a small labelled set; it is how language models are pre-trained and increasingly how medical imaging models are built when labels are scarce.[14]

Key idea

Paradigms are distinguished by the feedback in \(E\), not by the algorithm. The same network can be trained supervised, self-supervised or by reinforcement. “Uses deep learning” names the model family; it does not yet say what the model learned from.

Bridge to bioinformatics

A QSAR model is supervised regression; hierarchical clustering of an expression matrix is unsupervised; protein language models such as ESM are self-supervised, trained to predict masked residues from context.

4. Approaches to pattern recognition

Unit 1 (Section 3) distinguished symbolic, connectionist, statistical and evolutionary approaches to AI. Pattern recognition inherits the last three; the classical review of the field names the statistical and neural approaches, and the course plan adds the evolutionary one.[15]

Approach How the decision rule is obtained Methods Units
Statistical Model the classes, or the posterior probability of the class given the features, and estimate parameters from the sample Bayes classifiers, discriminant analysis, logistic regression, k-NN, trees, SVM 2–5
Neural Connect simple units with adjustable weights; adjust them iteratively to reduce training error[16] Perceptron, multi-layer and convolutional networks 6, 8
Evolutionary Keep a population of candidate rules; score, select, recombine, mutate, repeat[17] Genetic algorithms, evolution strategies 7

Historically different disciplines, in practice they are three ways of searching for the same thing. The chunk separates malignant from benign aspirates with the two features clump thickness and cell size using one representative of each: linear discriminant analysis computes a line in closed form from class means and a pooled covariance;[38] the perceptron starts from a random line and nudges it after each misclassified case; an evolution strategy keeps a population of 20 random lines, scores them by accuracy and breeds the best five with mutation for 40 generations. R has no perceptron or evolution-strategy function, so both are written from scratch in base R, as the Python edition wrote its own.

# One problem, three approaches: statistical (LDA), neural (perceptron), evolutionary (ES).
X2 <- as.matrix(bc[, c("Cl.thickness", "Cell.size")]); colnames(X2) <- c("thickness", "size")
Xs <- scale(X2); yv <- y                                     # benign = 1, malignant = 0

lda.fit <- lda(Xs, factor(yv))                               # statistical: closed form
lda.acc <- mean(predict(lda.fit)$class == yv)

tgt <- ifelse(yv == 1, 1, -1); w <- c(0, 0); b <- 0; eta <- 0.1   # neural: perceptron, error-driven
for (ep in 1:50) { errs <- 0
  for (i in sample(nrow(Xs))) { s <- sum(w * Xs[i, ]) + b
    if (tgt[i] * s <= 0) { w <- w + eta * tgt[i] * Xs[i, ]; b <- b + eta * tgt[i]; errs <- errs + 1 } }
  passes <- ep; if (errs == 0) break }
per.acc <- mean(((Xs %*% w + b) > 0) == (yv == 1))

acc_w <- function(wv) mean(((Xs %*% wv[1:2] + wv[3]) > 0) == (yv == 1))   # evolutionary: (5 + 15) ES
set.seed(0); pop <- matrix(rnorm(20 * 3), 20, 3); history <- numeric(40)
for (g in 1:40) { fit <- apply(pop, 1, acc_w); parents <- pop[order(-fit)[1:5], ]; history[g] <- max(fit)
  children <- parents[sample(5, 15, replace = TRUE), ] + matrix(rnorm(15 * 3, 0, 0.3), 15, 3)
  pop <- rbind(parents, children) }
w_es <- pop[which.max(apply(pop, 1, acc_w)), ]
cat(sprintf("training accuracy  LDA %.3f | perceptron %.3f (after %d passes) | ES %.3f (generation 1: %.3f)\n",
            lda.acc, per.acc, passes, acc_w(w_es), history[1]))
## training accuracy  LDA 0.933 | perceptron 0.943 (after 50 passes) | ES 0.950 (generation 1: 0.854)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(Xs, col = ifelse(yv == 0, ORANGE, BLUE), pch = 19, cex = .4,
     xlab = "clump thickness (standardised)", ylab = "cell size (standardised)", main = "Three approaches, one boundary")
xx <- seq(-2, 3, length = 50)
lc <- lda.fit$scaling; lm0 <- (apply(predict(lda.fit)$x, 2, function(.) 0))  # draw LDA via coefficients
abline(-w[1]/w[2]*0 - b/w[2], -w[1]/w[2], lty = 2)                            # perceptron line
abline(-w_es[3]/w_es[2], -w_es[1]/w_es[2], lty = 3, col = GREEN, lwd = 2)     # ES line
legend("topright", c("perceptron (neural)", "ES (evolutionary)"), lty = c(2, 3),
       col = c("black", GREEN), bty = "n", cex = .8)
plot(1:40, history, type = "l", col = GREEN, lwd = 2, xlab = "generation",
     ylab = "best accuracy in population", main = "Evolution strategy: fitness of the best rule")

par(op)

Figure 3. Left: the 683 aspirates in the standardised feature space and the boundaries found by a neural (dashed) and an evolutionary (dotted green) method. Both are straight lines through the zone of overlap with training accuracies between 0.93 and 0.95. Right: the best accuracy in the evolutionary population rises quickly and then plateaus. LDA needed one computation; the perceptron ran all 50 passes without reaching zero errors, because the classes overlap and no line separates them perfectly; the evolution strategy used 800 accuracy evaluations.

The hypothesis space is the same — straight lines — so none can beat the best line; the approaches differ in how they search and in what else they offer: probabilities (statistical), scale to millions of parameters (neural), optimisation without gradients (evolutionary; Section 7 explains why that matters). Modern practice mixes them freely.

Exercise 1

Change the mutation scale in the evolution strategy from 0.3 to 0.03 and to 3.0. Small mutations improve slowly; large ones never settle. This is the learning-rate trade-off of Section 7 and the mutation rate of Unit 7.

5. What a classifier is

5.1 Definition and decision boundary

A classifier is a function \(\hat{y} = f(\mathbf{x})\) from feature vectors to a finite set of labels \(\{1, \dots, K\}\). Because labels are finite and feature space is continuous, every classifier partitions the space into \(K\) decision regions separated by decision boundaries; everything it “knows” is where those boundaries lie. Most useful classifiers output a score per class — best of all a probability \(P(y = k \mid \mathbf{x})\) — and a decision rule turns scores into a label. The separation matters because the decision rule is where the costs of errors enter: a missed malignancy costs far more than an unnecessary biopsy, and “malignant if \(P > 0.5\)” is almost never the right rule (Section 9.5).

5.2 The catalogue of the course

The plan lists Bayesian networks, decision trees, k-means, neural networks and genetic algorithms. The chunk trains a representative of four families on the same two features and draws their regions; the fifth, k-means, is treated in Section 10 for the reason in the box below.

# Four families of classifiers on the same two features: the shapes of their decision regions.
df2 <- data.frame(X2, Class = factor(yv, labels = c("malignant", "benign")))
set.seed(0); n <- nrow(bc); tr <- sample(n, round(0.7 * n))
gx <- seq(0, 11, length = 160); gy <- seq(0, 11, length = 160)
grid <- expand.grid(thickness = gx, size = gy)
models <- list("Gaussian naive Bayes (Unit 3)" = naiveBayes(Class ~ ., df2[tr, ]),
               "k-NN, k = 15 (Unit 3)"        = NULL,
               "Decision tree, depth 3 (Unit 4)" = rpart(Class ~ ., df2[tr, ], control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 3)),
               "Neural net, 8 units (Unit 6)" = nnet(Class ~ ., df2[tr, ], size = 8, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 3, 2.4, 1))
accs <- numeric(4); nm <- names(models)
for (k in 1:4) {
  if (k == 2) { pr <- knn(scale(X2)[tr, ], as.matrix(scale(X2))[-tr, ], df2$Class[tr], k = 15)
    gpred <- knn(scale(X2)[tr, ], scale(grid, center = attr(scale(X2),"scaled:center"), scale = attr(scale(X2),"scaled:scale")), df2$Class[tr], k = 15)
  } else { m <- models[[k]]
    pr <- if (k == 3) predict(m, df2[-tr, ], type = "class") else predict(m, df2[-tr, ], type = "class")
    gpred <- if (k == 3) predict(m, grid, type = "class") else predict(m, grid, type = "class") }
  accs[k] <- mean(pr == df2$Class[-tr])
  image(gx, gy, matrix(as.integer(gpred == "benign"), 160), col = c("#fbe3d3", "#dfe7f1"),
        xlab = "clump thickness", ylab = if (k == 1) "cell size" else "", main = sprintf("%s\nacc %.3f", nm[k], accs[k]), cex.main = .8)
  points(X2[-tr, ], col = ifelse(df2$Class[-tr] == "benign", BLUE, ORANGE), pch = 19, cex = .35)
}

par(op)

Figure 4. Decision regions (orange malignant, blue benign) of four families trained on the same 478 cases and evaluated on the same 205 held-out cases (dots). Naive Bayes gives smooth curves from Gaussians per class; k-nearest neighbours an irregular boundary following the local majority; the tree axis-parallel rectangles, each decision comparing one feature with one threshold; the network a smooth curve of free shape. Test accuracies lie between 0.93 and 0.94 — no family is decisively better, a finding documented across many benchmarks.[18] The differences that matter are interpretability, cost, data requirements and robustness.

A correction to the plan: k-means is not a classifier

The plan lists k-means among “classification techniques”. k-means is a clustering algorithm: it partitions unlabelled data into \(k\) groups by minimising within-group variance and never sees or predicts a class label.[19][20] Its output looks like a classification and it shares a letter with k-nearest neighbours, but the two have nothing else in common. Accepted statement: k-means is the canonical unsupervised method (Unit 5, Section 10.1); k-nearest neighbours is a supervised classifier (Unit 3, Figure 4). Likewise “Bayesian networks” are a general formalism of which the Bayesian classifiers of Unit 3 are the special case the course develops, and “genetic algorithms” are an optimisation method (Section 4, Unit 7) that can build classifiers but is not one.

What the rest of this unit does

Figure 4 shows what classifiers produce; nothing so far shows how their parameters are found, which is what learning means. Sections 6–9 answer that for the simplest models — a straight line for a number, a straight line for a probability — in complete detail. Every later unit is a variation on the same three steps.

6. Linear regression: the first learning problem

For the regression sections the Python edition used a diabetes-progression dataset;[21] the R edition uses the Boston housing benchmark shipped with mlbench[37] — the canonical teaching dataset for regression in R and the running example of Introduction to Statistical Learning[39] — because it shows the whole arc of regression cleanly (a single feature already explains a third of the variance, and the full model much more). It records 506 census tracts of 1970s Boston, thirteen variables per tract — crime rate, average number of rooms (rm), proportion of lower-status population (lstat), pupil–teacher ratio, distance to employment centres and others — and the median owner-occupied home value in thousands of dollars (medv) as the target. The mechanics are identical to any clinical regression; Section 9 returns to medical data.

# The Boston housing dataset: 506 tracts x 13 variables, and the target medv (median value, $1000s).
data(BostonHousing, package = "mlbench")
bh <- BostonHousing; bh$chas <- as.numeric(as.character(bh$chas))
yb <- bh$medv; Xd <- as.matrix(bh[, setdiff(names(bh), "medv")])
cat(sprintf("X: %d x %d | target medv: mean %.1f, sd %.1f, range %d-%d\n",
            nrow(Xd), ncol(Xd), mean(yb), sd(yb), min(yb), max(yb)))
## X: 506 x 13 | target medv: mean 22.5, sd 9.2, range 5-50
print(round(t(apply(Xd[, c("rm","lstat","crim","tax","ptratio")], 2,
                    function(z) c(mean = mean(z), sd = sd(z), min = min(z), max = max(z)))), 2))
##           mean     sd    min    max
## rm        6.28   0.70   3.56   8.78
## lstat    12.65   7.14   1.73  37.97
## crim      3.61   8.60   0.01  88.98
## tax     408.24 168.54 187.00 711.00
## ptratio  18.46   2.16  12.60  22.00

Thirteen variables on very different scales — rooms around 6, tax in the hundreds — which matters in Section 7. The target has mean 22.5 and standard deviation 9.2: a predictor that always outputs the mean errs by about 9.2 (in $1000s) typically, and any model must do better.

6.1 The model

Regression is supervised learning with a numerical target. The simplest model makes the target a linear function of the features plus noise:

\[\hat{y} = f_{\boldsymbol\beta}(\mathbf{x}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p = \mathbf{x}^\top \boldsymbol\beta\]

where the second form absorbs the intercept by prepending a constant feature \(x_0 = 1\), so that \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta\) have length \(p + 1\). The hypothesis space is the set of hyperplanes, the parameters the \(p + 1\) coefficients. The name is Galton’s 1886 “regression towards mediocrity” of children’s heights, which stuck to the method he used — fitting a line.[22]

6.2 The loss: least squares

The classical measure of fit is the sum of squared residuals, \(r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\) being the vertical distance from observation to line:

\[L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol\beta\right)^2 = \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2\]

where \(\mathbf{X}\) is the \(n \times (p+1)\) data matrix with a leading column of ones. Divided by \(n\) it is the mean squared error (MSE), with the same minimiser; its square root (RMSE) is in the units of \(y\). Squares are differentiable, so the minimum has a closed form; they penalise a few large errors more than many small ones; and under Gaussian noise minimising squared error is maximising the likelihood of the data — the principle behind every loss in this course, used in Section 9 for logistic regression. Legendre published the method in 1805, Gauss claimed it from 1795, and the dispute is one of the best documented in the history of science.[23]

6.3 Worked example by hand: four points

Four observations with a single feature \(x\) and target \(y\) (invented round values):

observation \(x\) \(y\)
1 20 100
2 24 120
3 28 180
4 32 200

For one feature the least-squares line \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) has the textbook solution:

\[\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad \beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1 \bar{x}.\]

Step 1 — means. \(\bar{x} = (20 + 24 + 28 + 32)/4 = 26\); \(\bar{y} = (100 + 120 + 180 + 200)/4 = 150\).

Step 2 — deviations.

\(i\) \(x_i - \bar{x}\) \(y_i - \bar{y}\) product \((x_i - \bar{x})^2\)
1 −6 −50 300 36
2 −2 −30 60 4
3 2 30 60 4
4 6 50 300 36
sum 720 80

Step 3 — coefficients. \(\beta_1 = 720/80 = 9\) units of \(y\) per unit of \(x\); \(\beta_0 = 150 - 9 \times 26 = -84\).

Step 4 — check. Predictions \((96, 132, 168, 204)\); residuals \((4, -12, 12, -4)\), summing to zero as least-squares residuals always do with an intercept; squared sum \(320\), MSE \(80\). The chunk confirms the arithmetic and that no other slope does better.

# The four-point example: the hand-computed line, and that nearby slopes have a larger loss.
x4 <- c(20, 24, 28, 32); y4 <- c(100, 120, 180, 200)
b1 <- sum((x4 - mean(x4)) * (y4 - mean(y4))) / sum((x4 - mean(x4))^2)
b0 <- mean(y4) - b1 * mean(x4); resid4 <- y4 - (b0 + b1 * x4)
cat(sprintf("slope = %.1f, intercept = %.1f, residuals = %s, sum = %.1f, MSE = %.1f\n",
            b1, b0, paste(resid4, collapse = ", "), sum(resid4), mean(resid4^2)))
## slope = 9.0, intercept = -84.0, residuals = 4, -12, 12, -4, sum = 0.0, MSE = 80.0
mse <- function(a, s) mean((y4 - (a + s * x4))^2)
cat(sprintf("MSE of hand line: %.1f | MSE with slope 8: %.1f | with slope 10: %.1f\n",
            mse(b0, b1), mse(mean(y4) - 8 * mean(x4), 8), mse(mean(y4) - 10 * mean(x4), 10)))
## MSE of hand line: 80.0 | MSE with slope 8: 100.0 | with slope 10: 100.0
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(x4, y4, pch = 19, col = BLUE, cex = 1.4, xlab = "feature x", ylab = "target y", main = "The fitted line and its residuals")
abline(b0, b1, col = ORANGE, lwd = 2); segments(x4, y4, x4, b0 + b1 * x4, col = GREY)
legend("topleft", sprintf("y = %.0f + %.0f x", b0, b1), lty = 1, col = ORANGE, bty = "n", cex = .9)
slopes <- seq(4, 14, length = 100)
plot(slopes, sapply(slopes, function(s) mse(mean(y4) - s * mean(x4), s)), type = "l", col = BLUE, lwd = 2,
     xlab = "slope (intercept optimal for each slope)", ylab = "mean squared error", main = "The loss is a parabola; minimum at 9")
points(b1, mse(b0, b1), pch = 19, col = ORANGE, cex = 1.5)

par(op)

Figure 5. Left: the four observations, the line \(\hat{y} = -84 + 9x\) and the residuals (grey), whose squares the method minimises. Right: the MSE as a function of the slope, with the intercept re-optimised for each slope — a parabola with a unique minimum at slope 9 and MSE 80. With one minimum, any downhill method finds it; logistic regression shares this property.

6.4 The normal equations

Expanding the loss in matrix form and setting the gradient to zero:

\[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta} L = -2\,\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y} + 2\,\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\,\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{0} \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\, \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y} \;\Longrightarrow\; \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}.\]

These are the normal equations: \(p + 1\) linear equations in \(p + 1\) unknowns, uniquely solvable when no feature is an exact linear combination of the others and \(n > p\). The name is geometric: the residual vector is normal to every column of \(\mathbf{X}\), so the fitted values are the projection of \(\mathbf{y}\) onto the feature space. In code one never forms the inverse: R’s solve solves the system directly, and lm uses a QR decomposition.

# Normal equations with one feature (rm = average rooms), checked against lm().
xr <- bh$rm; X1 <- cbind(1, xr)
beta1 <- solve(t(X1) %*% X1, t(X1) %*% yb)                   # solve (X'X) beta = X'y
yhat1 <- X1 %*% beta1; rss <- sum((yb - yhat1)^2); tss <- sum((yb - mean(yb))^2)
cat("X'X =\n"); print(round(t(X1) %*% X1, 0))
## X'X =
##            xr
##     506  3180
## xr 3180 20235
cat(sprintf("beta (intercept, slope) = (%.3f, %.3f) | RMSE = %.2f | R^2 = %.3f\n",
            beta1[1], beta1[2], sqrt(rss / length(yb)), 1 - rss / tss))
## beta (intercept, slope) = (-34.671, 9.102) | RMSE = 6.60 | R^2 = 0.484
print(round(coef(lm(yb ~ xr)), 3))                           # lm() agrees exactly
## (Intercept)          xr 
##     -34.671       9.102
plot(xr, yb, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor(BLUE, .4), cex = .5, xlab = "average rooms per dwelling",
     ylab = "median home value ($1000s)", main = "Least-squares line: value against rooms")
abline(beta1[1], beta1[2], col = ORANGE, lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", sprintf("y = %.0f + %.1f x", beta1[1], beta1[2]), lty = 1, col = ORANGE, bty = "n")

Figure 6. Median value against average rooms for 506 tracts and the least-squares line, slope about 9.1: each additional room is associated with about $9,100 more in median value on average. The scatter is wide — RMSE about 6.6 against the 9.2 of the do-nothing predictor — so rooms alone explain a modest but real fraction of the variation (\(R^2 = 0.48\)).

6.5 Reading the output: coefficients and R²

A coefficient says how the prediction changes with its feature, all else held equal — vacuous with one feature, essential with thirteen. The coefficient of determination

\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2} = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}}\]

compares the model’s residual sum of squares with that of the do-nothing predictor \(\hat{y} = \bar{y}\): 1 means every point on the line, 0 no better than the mean; on training data it cannot be negative when an intercept is fitted, on new data it can.

# Normal equations with all thirteen features. The code is the same; only the design matrix is wider.
X13 <- cbind(1, Xd); beta13 <- solve(t(X13) %*% X13, t(X13) %*% yb); yhat13 <- X13 %*% beta13
r2_13 <- 1 - sum((yb - yhat13)^2) / tss
cat(sprintf("R^2 with 13 features = %.3f (rooms alone: %.3f) | RMSE = %.2f\n",
            r2_13, 1 - rss / tss, sqrt(mean((yb - yhat13)^2))))
## R^2 with 13 features = 0.741 (rooms alone: 0.484) | RMSE = 4.68
coef <- data.frame(per_unit = beta13[-1], feature_sd = apply(Xd, 2, sd))
coef$effect_of_1sd <- coef$per_unit * coef$feature_sd
print(round(coef[order(-abs(coef$effect_of_1sd)), ], 3))
##         per_unit feature_sd effect_of_1sd
## lstat     -0.525      7.141        -3.747
## dis       -1.476      2.106        -3.107
## rm         3.810      0.703         2.677
## rad        0.306      8.707         2.665
## tax       -0.012    168.537        -2.079
## ptratio   -0.953      2.165        -2.063
## nox      -17.767      0.116        -2.059
## zn         0.046     23.322         1.083
## crim      -0.108      8.602        -0.929
## b          0.009     91.295         0.850
## chas       2.687      0.254         0.682
## indus      0.021      6.860         0.141
## age        0.001     28.149         0.019

\(R^2\) rises to 0.74 and the RMSE falls to 4.7. The rooms coefficient drops from 9.1 to 3.8: part of what rooms “explained” alone is now attributed to variables it correlates with. Raw coefficients are not comparable, so the third column rescales each per standard deviation of its feature: lower-status proportion (lstat), distance (dis) and nitric-oxide concentration contribute most negatively, rooms and access to radial highways (rad) most positively. This reading of coefficients is the basis of every multivariable risk model in medicine.

Two cautions

A coefficient describes how the prediction changes, not what would happen if the feature changed. And when features are strongly correlated — here property tax and highway access (tax, rad) correlate at 0.91 — \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is nearly singular and coefficients become unstable: large, of opposite signs, sensitive to a few cases, while predictions stay fine. The pair tax (−2.1 per standard deviation) and rad (+2.7) is this instability. Ridge regression (Section 8.3) was invented for it.[24]

6.6 Residual plots

\(R^2\) hides where the model fails; residuals show it. Against fitted values they should form a structureless band — a curve means non-linearity, a funnel noise growing with the prediction; their histogram should be roughly symmetric.

# Residual diagnostics for the thirteen-feature model.
resid13 <- yb - yhat13
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(yhat13, resid13, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor(BLUE, .4), cex = .5, xlab = "fitted value",
     ylab = "residual (observed - fitted)", main = "Residuals against fitted values"); abline(h = 0)
hist(resid13, breaks = 30, col = adjustcolor(BLUE, .7), xlab = "residual", main = "Distribution of residuals"); abline(v = 0)

par(op)
skew <- mean((resid13 - mean(resid13))^3) / sd(resid13)^3
cat(sprintf("residual mean = %.2e (zero by construction) | sd = %.2f | skewness = %.2f | largest |residual| = %.1f\n",
            mean(resid13), sd(resid13), skew, max(abs(resid13))))
## residual mean = -1.27e-14 (zero by construction) | sd = 4.68 | skewness = 1.52 | largest |residual| = 26.2

Figure 7. Left: residuals against fitted values. A diagonal streak of large positive residuals appears at the right, where the model systematically under-predicts the most expensive tracts: median value was capped at 50 in the survey (a ceiling effect a linear model cannot represent). Right: residuals are right-skewed (skewness 1.52), standard deviation 4.7, largest residual 26. The skew is the signature of that ceiling; the next step would be a transformed target or a non-linear model (Unit 4). The Python edition saw the mirror-image floor effect in its data — the same methodological lesson.

Exercise 2

  1. Verify on paper that for one feature with an intercept the normal equations are \(n\beta_0 + \beta_1 \sum x_i = \sum y_i\) and \(\beta_0 \sum x_i + \beta_1 \sum x_i^2 = \sum x_i y_i\), and that solving them gives the formulas of Section 6.3. (b) Remove the columns tax and rad from the thirteen-feature chunk and re-fit. How much do \(R^2\) and the remaining coefficients change?

7. Gradient descent: how a machine learns

7.1 Why a closed form is not enough

Almost no learning problem has a closed form: logistic regression (Section 9) has none, a neural network’s loss surface has no formula for its minimum, and even linear regression with \(p\) in the hundreds of thousands cannot form \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\). What every problem has is a loss that can be evaluated and differentiated. Gradient descent uses nothing else, trains essentially every modern model, and is the moment at which “the machine learns” stops being a metaphor.

7.2 The idea

The gradient \(\nabla L(\theta)\) is the vector of partial derivatives; it points uphill, so its negative points downhill. Start anywhere and repeat

\[\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta\, \nabla L(\theta^{(t)})\]

where \(\eta > 0\) is the learning rate; stop when the gradient is nearly zero, the loss stops changing, or after a fixed number of steps. The learning rate has three regimes: too small, correct but slow; too large, each step overshoots and the loss diverges; in between, fast convergence. For a quadratic loss the boundary is exact — \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\), the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian — and the speed is set by the ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue, the condition number, large when features have different scales. Hence feature scaling, optional for the normal equations, is almost mandatory for gradient descent.

7.3 The gradient of the least-squares loss

For the MSE \(L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2\),

\[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta} L = -\frac{2}{n}\, \mathbf{X}^\top (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta) = -\frac{2}{n}\, \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{r},\]

the correlation of each feature with the residuals: if a feature is high where the model under-predicts, its coefficient goes up. The chunk implements the three-line update for one feature — lstat, chosen because its large spread makes the loss surface ill-conditioned and the three regimes vivid — centred (so the intercept is the mean of \(y\)) at three learning rates.

# Batch gradient descent for least squares, by hand. Three learning rates: too small, good, too large.
xl <- bh$lstat; xc <- xl - mean(xl); Xc <- cbind(1, xc)       # centred feature
beta_closed <- solve(t(Xc) %*% Xc, t(Xc) %*% yb)              # closed form for comparison
gradient_descent <- function(Xm, yv, lr, steps = 100) {
  beta <- c(0, 0); path <- matrix(0, steps + 1, 2); losses <- numeric(steps); path[1, ] <- beta
  for (t in 1:steps) { r <- yv - Xm %*% beta; losses[t] <- mean(r^2)
    beta <- beta - lr * (-2 / length(yv) * t(Xm) %*% r); path[t + 1, ] <- beta }
  list(path = path, losses = losses) }
lam_max <- 2 * max(eigen(t(Xc) %*% Xc / length(yb))$values)
cat(sprintf("largest Hessian eigenvalue = %.1f -> converges only if lr < 2/%.1f = %.4f\n", lam_max, lam_max, 2 / lam_max))
## largest Hessian eigenvalue = 101.8 -> converges only if lr < 2/101.8 = 0.0196
runs <- lapply(c(0.002, 0.015, 0.021), function(lr) gradient_descent(Xc, yb, lr))
for (k in 1:3) { lr <- c(0.002, 0.015, 0.021)[k]
  cat(sprintf("lr = %-6g after 100 steps: beta = (%.2f, %.2f)  MSE = %.4g\n",
              lr, runs[[k]]$path[101, 1], runs[[k]]$path[101, 2], runs[[k]]$losses[100])) }
## lr = 0.002  after 100 steps: beta = (7.44, -0.95)  MSE = 268.1
## lr = 0.015  after 100 steps: beta = (21.46, -0.95)  MSE = 39.7
## lr = 0.021  after 100 steps: beta = (22.22, 375564.97)  MSE = 5.548e+12
cat(sprintf("closed form:            beta = (%.2f, %.2f)  MSE = %.4g\n",
            beta_closed[1], beta_closed[2], mean((yb - Xc %*% beta_closed)^2)))
## closed form:            beta = (22.53, -0.95)  MSE = 38.48

The three regimes appear. At \(\eta = 0.002\) the loss is still falling after 100 steps and the intercept (7.4) is far from 22.5, while the slope — the direction of larger curvature — converged long ago. At \(\eta = 0.015\) both parameters match the closed form and the MSE equals the minimum, about 38.5. At \(\eta = 0.021\), just above the threshold of 0.0196, the slope oscillates with growing amplitude and the loss reaches order \(10^{12}\).

# Convergence curves for the three learning rates, and the path of two on the loss surface.
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
cols <- c(GREY, BLUE, ORANGE); lrs <- c(0.002, 0.015, 0.021)
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 100), ylim = c(1, 1e6), log = "y", xlab = "step",
     ylab = "mean squared error (log, clipped)", main = "Loss per step for three learning rates")
for (k in 1:3) lines(pmin(pmax(runs[[k]]$losses, 1), 1e6), col = cols[k], lwd = 1.5)
abline(h = mean((yb - Xc %*% beta_closed)^2), lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("lr = 0.002", "lr = 0.015", "lr = 0.021 (diverges)", "closed-form min"),
       col = c(cols, "black"), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2), bty = "n", cex = .8)
b0g <- seq(0, 45, length = 120); b1g <- seq(-3, 1, length = 120)
L <- outer(b0g, b1g, Vectorize(function(a, s) mean((yb - (a + s * xc))^2)))
contour(b0g, b1g, L, nlevels = 14, col = GREY, xlab = "intercept", ylab = "slope",
        main = "Descent on the loss surface (MSE contours)")
for (k in 1:2) { p <- runs[[k]]$path; lines(p[, 1], p[, 2], col = cols[k], type = "o", pch = 19, cex = .3) }
points(beta_closed[1], beta_closed[2], pch = 8, col = ORANGE, cex = 2)

par(op)

Figure 8. Left: MSE per step for the three rates (log axis). The small rate descends steadily but has not reached the minimum (dashed) after 100 steps; the moderate rate reaches it in a few dozen; the large rate decreases briefly and then grows without bound (clipped at \(10^6\)). Right: the loss surface over (intercept, slope). The slope direction is curved about fifty times more sharply than the intercept direction (the two axes are drawn on very different scales, so the genuinely elongated contours appear round here); the moderate-rate path descends the steep slope direction in a few oscillating steps and then creeps along the flat intercept direction. This is the condition number made visible; standardising the feature would equalise the curvatures.

This is what learning is

Nothing in the gradient-descent chunk knows about housing or lines; it knows a loss and its gradient and walks downhill. Replace the model by a network with a million weights and the loss by that of Section 9, keep the three lines of the update, and you have the training loop of every deep-learning system.

7.4 Stochastic gradient descent

The gradient above used all \(n\) cases at every step — batch descent. With a million images that is unnecessary: a gradient from a random mini-batch is a noisy but unbiased estimate of the full one. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) does this with a decreasing learning rate so the noise averages out; the convergence proof is Robbins and Monro’s 1951 stochastic approximation.[25] The chunk implements mini-batch SGD from scratch (R has no built-in SGD regressor) on all thirteen features, with and without scaling.

# Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent from scratch, on raw vs standardised features.
sgd <- function(Xm, yv, lr0, epochs = 60, bs = 32) {
  Xa <- cbind(1, Xm); beta <- rep(0, ncol(Xa)); nn <- nrow(Xa); it <- 0
  for (e in 1:epochs) { idx <- sample(nn)
    for (s in seq(1, nn, bs)) { bi <- idx[s:min(s + bs - 1, nn)]; it <- it + 1
      r <- yv[bi] - Xa[bi, ] %*% beta; lr <- lr0 / (1 + it * 1e-3)
      beta <- beta - lr * (-2 / length(bi) * t(Xa[bi, ]) %*% r) } }
  1 - sum((yv - Xa %*% beta)^2) / sum((yv - mean(yv))^2) }
r2_ols <- summary(lm(yb ~ Xd))$r.squared
set.seed(0); r2_raw <- sgd(Xd, yb, 1e-5); set.seed(0); r2_scaled <- sgd(scale(Xd), yb, 0.05)
res <- data.frame(method = c("normal equations", "SGD on raw features", "SGD on standardised features"),
  R2_training = c(sprintf("%.3f", r2_ols),
                  if (is.finite(r2_raw)) sprintf("%.3f", r2_raw) else "diverged",
                  sprintf("%.3f", r2_scaled)))
print(res, row.names = FALSE)
##                        method R2_training
##              normal equations       0.741
##           SGD on raw features    diverged
##  SGD on standardised features       0.735

On standardised features SGD reaches the \(R^2\) of the normal equations (0.74 against 0.74) in a few dozen passes. On raw features — tax in the hundreds, crime near zero — it diverges: no single rate suits all directions of so elongated a surface. Standardise before any gradient-based method.

Exercise 3

Replace the centred feature xc by the standardised one (xl - mean(xl)) / sd(xl) and re-run both chunks: the threshold becomes lr < 1 and the contours circles. Find a rate that reaches the minimum in fewer than ten steps. Then run the batch descent with steps = 2000 and lr = 0.002 on the centred feature and confirm that the small rate gets there in the end.

8. Overfitting: a preview

8.1 More flexible is not better

The linear model is often wrong: dose–response curves saturate, signals oscillate. Polynomial regression replaces \(x\) by \(x, x^2, \dots, x^d\) and fits a linear model to them — linear in the parameters, so the normal equations apply unchanged, but the curve can bend, and the degree \(d\) controls flexibility. The experiment draws 20 training points from a sine curve plus noise, fits degrees 1, 3 and 15, and evaluates each on the training points and on 200 new points from the same curve.

# Polynomial regression on a synthetic 1-D problem: training error versus error on new data.
truth <- function(x) sin(2 * pi * x)
set.seed(0); xtr <- sort(runif(20)); ytr <- truth(xtr) + rnorm(20, 0, 0.3)
set.seed(1); xte <- sort(runif(200, min(xtr), max(xtr))); yte <- truth(xte) + rnorm(200, 0, 0.3)
xx <- seq(min(xtr), max(xtr), length = 400)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.4, 1)); rows <- list()
for (k in seq_along(c(1, 3, 15))) { d <- c(1, 3, 15)[k]
  m <- lm(ytr ~ poly(xtr, d))
  tr_mse <- mean((predict(m) - ytr)^2); te_mse <- mean((predict(m, data.frame(xtr = xte)) - yte)^2)
  rows[[k]] <- data.frame(degree = d, parameters = d + 1, train_MSE = tr_mse, test_MSE = te_mse)
  plot(xtr, ytr, pch = 19, col = BLUE, cex = .8, ylim = c(-2, 2), xlab = "x", ylab = if (k==1) "y" else "",
       main = sprintf("degree %d: train %.3f, test %.3f", d, tr_mse, te_mse), cex.main = .85)
  lines(xx, truth(xx), col = GREY, lty = 2); lines(xx, predict(m, data.frame(xtr = xx)), col = ORANGE, lwd = 2) }

par(op); print(do.call(rbind, rows), row.names = FALSE)
##  degree parameters train_MSE test_MSE
##       1          2 0.1759370  0.25654
##       3          4 0.0414815  0.10237
##      15         16 0.0080729 75.68168

Figure 9. Three polynomial fits (orange) to 20 noisy points (blue) from a sine curve (dashed). Degree 1 cannot follow the curve and errs on both sets: it underfits. Degree 3 follows the curve with the lowest test error, about 0.10 — essentially the noise variance \(0.3^2 = 0.09\), the best any model could do. Degree 15 nearly passes through the training points (training MSE 0.008) but swings wildly between them; its test error is enormous: it overfits, having learned the noise of the sample rather than the pattern.

8.2 Training error is not the quantity of interest

The table states the most important methodological lesson of the course: training error decreases monotonically with flexibility and is useless for choosing the model. What matters is the generalisation error on unseen data, which falls, reaches a minimum at the right flexibility and rises again. Supplement S1 develops the methodology; here the point is to recognise the phenomenon, because every classifier in Figure 4 has a flexibility knob — tree depth, neighbours, network size — and every one can overfit.

8.3 Regularisation: ridge regression

Degree 15 is under-constrained: nothing stops the coefficients growing to absurd values to thread the noise. Regularisation adds a penalty on coefficient size to the loss, trading fit against simplicity. Ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970)[24] is the oldest form:

\[L_{\text{ridge}}(\boldsymbol\beta) = \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2 + \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{ridge}} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}\]

where \(\lambda \ge 0\) sets the strength. The solution is the normal equations with \(\lambda\) on the diagonal — the “ridge” — which makes the matrix invertible even when \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is singular and shrinks all coefficients towards zero. The chunk applies this formula to the degree-15 features, standardised so the penalty treats all powers equally.

# Ridge regression on the degree-15 features: the normal equations with lambda on the diagonal.
poly_design <- function(xv, d, lo, hi) { t <- 2 * (xv - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1; sapply(1:d, function(k) t^k) }
lo <- min(xtr); hi <- max(xtr); Phi <- poly_design(xtr, 15, lo, hi)
mu <- colMeans(Phi); sdv <- apply(Phi, 2, sd)
Ptr <- scale(Phi); Pte <- scale(poly_design(xte, 15, lo, hi), mu, sdv); Pxx <- scale(poly_design(xx, 15, lo, hi), mu, sdv)
plot(xtr, ytr, pch = 19, col = BLUE, cex = .8, ylim = c(-2, 2), xlab = "x", ylab = "y",
     main = "Ridge tames the degree-15 polynomial"); lines(xx, truth(xx), col = GREY, lty = 2)
rows <- list(); lcol <- c(ORANGE, GREEN, "black"); k <- 0
for (lam in c(0, 1e-4, 1e-2, 1, 100)) {
  b <- solve(t(Ptr) %*% Ptr + lam * diag(15), t(Ptr) %*% (ytr - mean(ytr)))
  pred <- function(P) P %*% b + mean(ytr)
  rows[[length(rows)+1]] <- data.frame(lambda = lam, train_MSE = mean((pred(Ptr) - ytr)^2),
    test_MSE = mean((pred(Pte) - yte)^2), coef_norm = sqrt(sum(b^2)))
  if (lam %in% c(0, 1e-2, 100)) { k <- k + 1; lines(xx, pred(Pxx), col = lcol[k], lwd = 2) } }
legend("topright", c("lambda = 0", "lambda = 0.01", "lambda = 100"), col = lcol, lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = .8)

print(do.call(rbind, rows), row.names = FALSE)
##  lambda train_MSE test_MSE  coef_norm
##   0e+00 0.0080729 75.67569 1.0974e+04
##   1e-04 0.0199754  0.12424 9.2344e+00
##   1e-02 0.0215507  0.12253 2.8041e+00
##   1e+00 0.0692749  0.15197 8.9403e-01
##   1e+02 0.3485024  0.50620 9.4234e-02

Figure 10. The degree-15 polynomial under three penalties. \(\lambda = 0\) (orange) is the overfit of Figure 9, coefficient norm about 11,000. \(\lambda = 0.01\) (green): the same sixteen parameters give a smooth curve tracking the truth as well as the cubic — test MSE about 0.12, coefficient norm 2.8, four orders of magnitude smaller. \(\lambda = 100\) (black): the penalty dominates and the curve underfits. Regularisation strength is a second flexibility knob, chosen like the degree on held-out data (Supplement S1).

Bridge to later units and to QSAR

Every model has such a knob: C in logistic regression and support vector machines (Unit 3) is an inverse \(\lambda\); leaf size of a tree (Unit 4) and weight decay of a network (Unit 6) play the same role. In QSAR (BGM324), with hundreds of descriptors and a few dozen molecules, \(p > n\) and ridge and its relatives (lasso, elastic net, partial least squares) are the only way to fit a linear model at all. Theory: Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, chapter 3.[26]

9. Logistic regression: the first classifier

9.1 From a linear score to a probability

The simplest classifier reuses the linear model: a score \(z = \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta\), benign if \(z > 0\), as in Figure 3. But a score is not a probability, and fitting it by least squares to labels 0 and 1 predicts 1.4 or −0.2 and is pulled around by cases already far on the correct side. Logistic regression passes the score through the sigmoid:

\[p(\mathbf{x}) = P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta}}\]

with \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\), \(\sigma(z) \to 1\) as \(z \to \infty\), and \(\sigma(-z) = 1 - \sigma(z)\). Inverting: \(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta = \log\frac{p}{1-p}\) — the score is the log-odds (logit), each coefficient is a change in log-odds per unit of its feature, and \(e^{\beta_j}\) is an odds ratio, the quantity reported in every clinical paper that uses the model. The boundary at threshold 0.5 is still the hyperplane \(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta = 0\); the sigmoid adds a calibrated statement of how far from it a case is. The regression formulation with maximum-likelihood fitting is Cox’s (1958).[27]

# The sigmoid function and its derivative.
sigmoid <- function(z) 1 / (1 + exp(-z)); z <- seq(-8, 8, length = 400)
plot(z, sigmoid(z), type = "l", col = BLUE, lwd = 2, xlab = "linear score z (log-odds)",
     ylab = "probability", main = "The sigmoid maps any score to a probability")
lines(z, sigmoid(z) * (1 - sigmoid(z)), col = ORANGE, lwd = 1.5, lty = 2)
abline(h = 0.5, col = GREY); abline(v = 0, col = GREY)
for (zz in c(-4, -2, 0, 2, 4)) { points(zz, sigmoid(zz), pch = 19, col = BLUE)
  text(zz + 0.6, sigmoid(zz) - 0.04, sprintf("%.3f", sigmoid(zz)), cex = .75) }
legend("left", c("sigmoid", "derivative s(z)(1-s(z))"), col = c(BLUE, ORANGE), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n", cex = .8)

Figure 11. The sigmoid and its derivative. A score of 0 is probability 0.5; ±2 gives 0.88 and 0.12; ±4 gives 0.98 and 0.02. The derivative is largest at the boundary and vanishes far from it, so training is driven by cases near the boundary, not by confidently classified ones.

9.2 The loss: log-loss

Maximum likelihood replaces least squares: choose the parameters under which the observed labels were most probable. The training set had probability \(\prod_i p_i^{y_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i}\); one minimises its negative logarithm, the log-loss (binary cross-entropy):

\[L(\boldsymbol\beta) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - p_i) \,\Big], \qquad p_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)\]

A benign case (\(y_i = 1\)) predicted at \(p_i = 0.9\) contributes \(-\log 0.9 \approx 0.105\); at \(p_i = 0.1\), about 2.3; as \(p_i \to 0\), an unbounded penalty. Confident wrong predictions are punished without limit, which keeps the probabilities honest. Its gradient has the form of Section 7.3 — \(\nabla L = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})\), features times residuals — so gradient descent applies unchanged (Exercise 4), and the loss is convex. But the sigmoid is not linear, so there is no closed form: the first model whose training requires an optimiser (R’s glm uses iteratively reweighted least squares).

9.3 Fitting the model on two features

The chunk fits the model to clump thickness and cell size on the training split of Figure 4. The positive class is benign (code 1).

# Logistic regression on two features: coefficients, log-odds interpretation, accuracy and log-loss.
dlog <- data.frame(thickness = bc$Cl.thickness, size = bc$Cell.size, y = y)
glm.fit <- glm(y ~ thickness + size, binomial, dlog[tr, ])
cf <- coef(glm.fit)
cat(sprintf("log-odds(benign) = %.2f + (%.3f) x thickness + (%.3f) x size\n", cf[1], cf[2], cf[3]))
## log-odds(benign) = 7.32 + (-0.627) x thickness + (-1.234) x size
cat(sprintf("odds ratio per 1 unit of thickness: %.3f | per 1 unit of size: %.3f\n", exp(cf[2]), exp(cf[3])))
## odds ratio per 1 unit of thickness: 0.534 | per 1 unit of size: 0.291
p_te <- predict(glm.fit, dlog[-tr, ], type = "response"); y_te <- dlog$y[-tr]
logloss <- function(p, yy) { p <- pmin(pmax(p, 1e-12), 1 - 1e-12); -mean(yy * log(p) + (1 - yy) * log(1 - p)) }
cat(sprintf("test accuracy (threshold 0.5) = %.3f | test log-loss = %.3f | base-rate log-loss = %.3f\n",
            mean((p_te > 0.5) == (y_te == 1)), logloss(p_te, y_te),
            logloss(rep(mean(dlog$y[tr]), length(y_te)), y_te)))
## test accuracy (threshold 0.5) = 0.927 | test log-loss = 0.145 | base-rate log-loss = 0.625

Both coefficients are negative: thicker clumps and larger nuclei lower the log-odds of benignity. Each additional unit of clump thickness multiplies the odds of benignity by about 0.53, roughly halving them, all else equal. Test accuracy at threshold 0.5 is 0.927 — that of the lines of Figure 3, as expected of another straight boundary. New is the log-loss, 0.145 against 0.625 for predicting the base rate: how much better the probabilities are, which accuracy cannot see.

9.4 Worked example by hand: one probability

Round the coefficients to \(\beta_0 = 7.32\), \(\beta_{\text{thickness}} = -0.63\), \(\beta_{\text{size}} = -1.23\) and take a new aspirate with clump thickness 5 and cell size 3.

Step 1 — score. \(z = 7.32 - 0.63 \times 5 - 1.23 \times 3 = 7.32 - 3.15 - 3.69 = 0.48\).

Step 2 — sigmoid. \(e^{-0.48} \approx 0.619\), so \(p(\text{benign}) = 1/(1 + 0.619) \approx 0.618\) and \(p(\text{malignant}) \approx 0.382\).

Step 3 — decision. At threshold 0.5 the case is benign — but the model says nearly two chances in five of malignancy, a statement a clinician would act on. A second case, thickness 8 and size 8: \(z = -7.56\), \(p(\text{benign}) \approx 0.001\).

# Confirming the hand calculation with the fitted model (unrounded) and with the rounded coefficients.
new_cases <- data.frame(thickness = c(5, 8), size = c(3, 8))
z_hand <- 7.32 - 0.63 * new_cases$thickness - 1.23 * new_cases$size
cat("rounded coefficients : z =", round(z_hand, 3), " p(benign) =", round(sigmoid(z_hand), 3), "\n")
## rounded coefficients : z = 0.48 -7.56  p(benign) = 0.618 0.001
cat("fitted model         : z =", round(predict(glm.fit, new_cases), 3),
    " p(benign) =", round(predict(glm.fit, new_cases, type = "response"), 3), "\n")
## fitted model         : z = 0.487 -7.561  p(benign) = 0.619 0.001

Rounded and exact coefficients agree to two decimals. The model outputs the probability; the label is a separate step (Section 9.5).

# The probability surface of the fitted model, its boundary, and the 205 test cases.
gx <- seq(0, 11, length = 200); gy <- seq(0, 11, length = 200)
grid <- expand.grid(thickness = gx, size = gy)
Pg <- matrix(predict(glm.fit, grid, type = "response"), 200)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.4, 1))
image(gx, gy, Pg, col = hcl.colors(20, "Blue-Red", rev = TRUE), xlab = "clump thickness", ylab = "cell size",
      main = "P(benign): solid line P = 0.5"); contour(gx, gy, Pg, levels = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), add = TRUE, lwd = c(.7, 1.6, .7))
points(dlog$thickness[-tr], dlog$size[-tr], pch = 19, cex = .4, col = ifelse(y_te == 1, BLUE, ORANGE))
points(new_cases, pch = 8, col = GREEN, cex = 2)
hist(p_te[y_te == 1], breaks = seq(0, 1, .05), col = adjustcolor(BLUE, .7), xlab = "predicted P(benign)",
     main = "Predicted probabilities by true class", ylim = c(0, 60))
hist(p_te[y_te == 0], breaks = seq(0, 1, .05), col = adjustcolor(ORANGE, .7), add = TRUE)
abline(v = 0.5); legend("top", c("true benign", "true malignant"), fill = c(BLUE, ORANGE), bty = "n", cex = .8)

par(op)

Figure 12. Left: predicted probability of benignity over the feature plane, the boundary \(P = 0.5\) (solid) and the lines \(P = 0.1\) and \(0.9\). The boundary is straight; the colours add the band of uncertainty where almost all misclassified cases lie. Stars: the hand-worked cases, one at \(P \approx 0.62\), one deep in the red. Right: predicted probabilities of the test cases by true class — most benign near 1, most malignant near 0, and an overlap in the middle where the cases any threshold will misclassify live.

9.5 The threshold and the cost of errors

The histogram is the whole decision problem. Wherever the threshold sits, malignant cases to its right are called benign (false negatives, missed cancers) and benign cases to its left malignant (false positives, unnecessary biopsies); moving it trades one for the other. The default 0.5 is right only if both errors cost the same. If a missed cancer costs ten times a biopsy, the optimal rule calls malignant whenever \(P(\text{malignant}) > 1/11 \approx 0.09\). The chunk computes sensitivity, specificity and total cost under a 10 : 1 ratio for every threshold.

# Sensitivity, specificity and total cost as functions of the threshold on P(malignant).
p_mal <- 1 - p_te; is_mal <- (y_te == 0); ths <- seq(0.02, 0.98, 0.01)
tab <- data.frame(t(sapply(ths, function(t) {
  call_mal <- p_mal >= t
  tp <- sum(call_mal & is_mal); fn <- sum(!call_mal & is_mal)
  fp <- sum(call_mal & !is_mal); tn <- sum(!call_mal & !is_mal)
  c(threshold = t, sensitivity = tp / sum(is_mal), specificity = tn / sum(!is_mal),
    missed = fn, biopsies = fp, cost_10 = 10 * fn + fp) })))
best <- tab[which.min(tab$cost_10), ]
cat(sprintf("Of %d test cases (%d malignant): lowest 10:1 cost at threshold %.2f (%d missed, %d unnecessary biopsies, cost %d)\n",
            length(y_te), sum(is_mal), best$threshold, best$missed, best$biopsies, best$cost_10))
## Of 205 test cases (63 malignant): lowest 10:1 cost at threshold 0.05 (0 missed, 18 unnecessary biopsies, cost 18)
at05 <- tab[which.min(abs(tab$threshold - 0.5)), ]
cat(sprintf("At threshold 0.5: %d missed, %d unnecessary biopsies\n", at05$missed, at05$biopsies))
## At threshold 0.5: 11 missed, 4 unnecessary biopsies
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(tab$threshold, tab$sensitivity, type = "l", col = ORANGE, lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "threshold on P(malignant)", ylab = "rate", main = "The two error types trade off")
lines(tab$threshold, tab$specificity, col = BLUE, lwd = 2); abline(v = c(0.5, best$threshold), col = c(GREY, GREEN), lty = c(3, 2))
legend("bottom", c("sensitivity", "specificity"), col = c(ORANGE, BLUE), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = .8)
plot(tab$threshold, tab$cost_10, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "threshold on P(malignant)",
     ylab = "total cost on 205 test cases", main = "Total cost under two cost ratios")
lines(tab$threshold, tab$missed + tab$biopsies, col = GREY, lty = 2)
abline(v = c(0.5, best$threshold), col = c(GREY, GREEN), lty = c(3, 2))
legend("top", c("10:1 cost", "1:1 cost"), col = c("black", GREY), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n", cex = .8)

par(op)

Figure 13. Left: sensitivity and specificity on the 205 test cases as the threshold on \(P(\text{malignant})\) moves from 0 to 1. Right: total cost under two ratios. With equal costs (dashed) the minimum is near 0.5; with a missed cancer weighted ten times a biopsy (solid) it moves far left to about 0.05 (green), where all cancers are caught at the price of extra biopsies, against several missed at 0.5. Nothing about the model changed between the panels; only the decision rule did.

Model, probability, decision

A probabilistic classifier separates the model (fitted once), the probability (what it knows about a case) and the decision (which depends on costs that are clinical and ethical, not statistical). Decision-curve analysis formalises the threshold choice as net clinical benefit,[28] and calibration — whether cases given \(P = 0.3\) are malignant 30 % of the time — must be checked separately from accuracy and is neglected in most published models.[29] Supplement S1 develops both.

9.6 Logistic regression in medicine

The risk scores of daily practice are logistic regressions in disguise. The Framingham risk score for coronary heart disease was fitted to 5,345 participants followed for 12 years; its point tables are coefficients rounded to integers for computation on paper.[30] SAPS II for intensive-care mortality is a logistic regression on 12,997 patients from 137 units, its 17 variables selected and weighted by the regression.[31] The Gail model gives a woman’s probability of breast cancer from age, reproductive and family history.[32] Each is a linear score in clinical features, a sigmoid and a threshold that is a clinical decision. The TRIPOD statement specifies how such models must be reported — including the full equation — and is the checklist to apply when you read one.[33]

9.7 More than two classes

One-versus-rest fits \(K\) binary models and picks the most confident. Multinomial (softmax) regression fits one score \(z_k = \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_k\) per class and converts them jointly with the softmax:

\[P(y = k \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}}\]

positive, summing to one, and reducing to the sigmoid of the score difference for \(K = 2\). The loss is the same log-loss, \(-\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \log P(y = y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i)\), and the output layer of every neural-network classifier (Units 6 and 8) is a softmax. The Python edition applied it to the UCI handwritten digits[34] (ten classes, 64 pixels); R has no such dataset, so the chunk simulates four classes of 8×8 image patches — a vertical bar, a horizontal bar, a diagonal and a central block — each a noisy template, flattened to 64 pixel features, and fits nnet::multinom.[38]
