# Multinomial (softmax) logistic regression on simulated 8x8 image patches: four classes, 64 pixels.
set.seed(0); amp <- 1.6; sig <- 1.5
gen <- function(cl) { m <- matrix(rnorm(64, 0, sig), 8, 8)
  if (cl == 1) m[, 4:5] <- m[, 4:5] + amp        # vertical bar
  if (cl == 2) m[4:5, ] <- m[4:5, ] + amp        # horizontal bar
  if (cl == 3) for (k in 1:8) m[k, k] <- m[k, k] + amp   # diagonal
  if (cl == 4) m[3:6, 3:6] <- m[3:6, 3:6] + amp  # central block
  as.vector(m) }
N <- 200; lab <- rep(1:4, each = N / 4); Xi <- t(sapply(lab, gen))
set.seed(0); tri <- sample(N, round(0.7 * N))
sm <- multinom(factor(lab[tri]) ~ ., data.frame(Xi[tri, ]), trace = FALSE, decay = 0.2, MaxNWts = 5000)
prob <- predict(sm, data.frame(Xi[-tri, ]), type = "probs"); pr <- predict(sm, data.frame(Xi[-tri, ]))
cat(sprintf("test accuracy on %d patches = %.3f | probabilities sum to one: %s | mean confidence = %.3f\n",
            N - length(tri), mean(pr == lab[-tri]), all(abs(rowSums(prob) - 1) < 1e-8), mean(apply(prob, 1, max))))
## test accuracy on 60 patches = 0.950 | probabilities sum to one: TRUE | mean confidence = 0.892
cm <- table(true = lab[-tri], predicted = pr)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.4, 1))
image(1:8, 1:8, matrix(gen(3), 8), col = grey.colors(20), xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "one simulated 'diagonal' patch")
image(1:4, 1:4, t(cm[4:1, ]), col = hcl.colors(12, "Blues", rev = TRUE), xlab = "predicted class",
      ylab = "true class", axes = FALSE, main = "Confusion matrix (60 test patches)")
axis(1, 1:4); axis(2, 1:4, labels = 4:1)
for (i in 1:4) for (j in 1:4) text(j, 5 - i, cm[i, j], col = ifelse(cm[i, j] > max(cm)/2, "white", "black"))

par(op)

Figure 14. Right: confusion matrix on 60 held-out simulated patches; rows true, columns predicted, diagonal correct. Accuracy is 0.95 — the linear softmax model misreads about one patch in twenty — and the off-diagonal entries show which confusions occur (the diagonal template occasionally read as the central block), information accuracy hides and that matters when some confusions are graver than others. Left: one noisy “diagonal” patch, to show how much noise the model sees through.

Exercise 4

  1. Implement gradient descent for logistic regression on the two standardised features: from \(\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{0}\), gradient \(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^\top(\sigma(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta) - \mathbf{y})\), rate 0.5, 500 steps; compare with glm on the same features. (b) Change the cost ratio in the threshold chunk to 3 and to 30. (c) Raise the image noise sig to 2.5 and watch the confusion matrix fill in.

10. Previews of the other paradigms

10.1 Unsupervised: k-means on the breast-cancer features, without labels

k-means partitions \(n\) points into \(k\) groups minimising squared distances to group centroids by an alternation worth tracing once by hand: (1) assign each point to the nearest centroid; (2) update each centroid to the mean of its points; repeat until nothing changes (Lloyd, 1957; MacQueen, 1967).[20][19] It is the nearest-centroid classifier of Unit 1 run without labels: it guesses the groups, computes centroids, re-guesses, iterates. The chunk runs it with \(k = 2\) on the two features — never seeing the diagnosis — and only then compares with the labels.

# k-means (k = 2) on two features of all 683 aspirates, labels hidden; then compared with the labels.
set.seed(0); km <- kmeans(X2, centers = 2, nstart = 10)          # X2 only: no labels
clusters <- km$cluster - 1
agreement <- max(mean(clusters == yv), mean(clusters != yv))     # cluster numbering is arbitrary
ct <- table(cluster = clusters, biopsy = ifelse(yv == 0, "malignant", "benign"))
cat("centroids found without labels:\n"); print(round(km$centers, 2))
## centroids found without labels:
##   thickness size
## 1      3.05 1.45
## 2      7.77 7.24
cat(sprintf("agreement between clusters and diagnosis (best label matching): %.3f = %d of %d\n",
            agreement, round(agreement * nrow(bc)), nrow(bc)))
## agreement between clusters and diagnosis (best label matching): 0.927 = 633 of 683
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.4, 1))
plot(X2, col = ifelse(clusters == round(mean(clusters[yv == 1])), BLUE, ORANGE), pch = 19, cex = .4,
     xlab = "clump thickness", ylab = "cell size", main = "What k-means found (no labels)")
points(km$centers, pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 3)
plot(X2, col = ifelse(yv == 1, BLUE, ORANGE), pch = 19, cex = .4, xlab = "clump thickness", ylab = "cell size",
     main = "The biopsy labels (blue benign)")

par(op); print(ct)
##        biopsy
## cluster benign malignant
##       0    438        44
##       1      6       195

Figure 15. Left: the two groups found from the features alone, with centroids (crosses). Right: the same points coloured by biopsy. The unsupervised algorithm recovered a partition agreeing with the pathologist for about 93 % of the aspirates (633 of 683), because the two diagnoses happen to form two dense regions and k-means finds dense regions; the cross-tabulation shows the cases on the wrong side of the gap.

Encouraging and a warning. Structure in unlabelled data can coincide with clinical categories — the hope behind every search for patient subtypes. But the agreement is near the supervised methods only because the classes separate cleanly here; the algorithm was told that two groups existed, and had the natural clusters been “large” and “small” tumours it would have found those and nothing in its output would have said so. Unit 5 treats the choice of \(k\) and the validation of a clustering.

10.2 Reinforcement: a five-state corridor

Positions 0 to 4; the agent starts at 2 and moves left or right. Position 0 is an exit with reward 0.3, position 4 an exit with reward 1.0; both end the episode; other moves earn nothing. One step from the small exit the agent faces the defining question: take 0.3 now, or walk three steps for 1.0? The answer depends on the discount factor \(\gamma \in [0, 1)\): a reward \(t\) steps away is worth \(\gamma^t\) of one now. The value \(V^*(s)\), the best discounted sum of future rewards from \(s\), satisfies Bellman’s equation:

\[V^*(s) = \max_{a} \Big[\, r(s, a) + \gamma\, V^*(s') \,\Big]\]

where \(s'\) is the state reached by action \(a\) and \(V^*\) of an exit is 0. Value iteration starts with \(V = 0\) and applies the right-hand side repeatedly until \(V\) stops changing; the optimal policy takes, in each state, the maximising action.[11]

Worked by hand, \(\gamma = 0.9\). Positions 1, 2, 3 have values to compute; start with \(V = (0, 0, 0)\).

sweep \(V(1) = \max(0.3,\; 0.9\,V(2))\) \(V(2) = \max(0.9\,V(1),\; 0.9\,V(3))\) \(V(3) = \max(0.9\,V(2),\; 1.0)\)
0 0 0 0
1 \(\max(0.3, 0) = 0.3\) \(\max(0, 0) = 0\) \(\max(0, 1.0) = 1.0\)
2 \(\max(0.3, 0) = 0.3\) \(\max(0.27, 0.9) = 0.9\) \(1.0\)
3 \(\max(0.3, 0.81) = 0.81\) \(0.9\) \(1.0\)
4 \(0.81\) \(0.9\) \(1.0\) — converged

\(V^* = (0.81, 0.9, 1.0)\) and the maximising action is “right” everywhere: the agent ignores the small exit even when next to it, because \(0.9^2 = 0.81 > 0.3\). With \(\gamma = 0.5\), position 1 gives \(\max(0.3, 0.25) = 0.3\) and the agent takes the small exit — a myopic agent settles for less.

# Value iteration on the five-state corridor, for two discount factors.
step <- function(s, a) { s2 <- s + a                               # move; returns (new state, reward, ended)
  if (s2 == 0) return(list(s2, 0.3, TRUE)); if (s2 == 4) return(list(s2, 1.0, TRUE)); list(s2, 0, FALSE) }
value_iteration <- function(gamma, tol = 1e-9) {
  V <- rep(0, 5); sweeps <- 0
  repeat { Vn <- V
    for (s in c(1, 2, 3)) Vn[s + 1] <- max(sapply(c(-1, 1), function(a) {
      r <- step(s, a); r[[2]] + gamma * (if (r[[3]]) 0 else V[r[[1]] + 1]) }))
    sweeps <- sweeps + 1; if (max(abs(Vn - V)) < tol) return(list(V = Vn, sweeps = sweeps)); V <- Vn } }
for (gamma in c(0.9, 0.5)) { out <- value_iteration(gamma)
  policy <- sapply(c(1, 2, 3), function(s) {
    rR <- step(s, 1); rL <- step(s, -1)
    vR <- rR[[2]] + gamma * (if (rR[[3]]) 0 else out$V[rR[[1]] + 1])
    vL <- rL[[2]] + gamma * (if (rL[[3]]) 0 else out$V[rL[[1]] + 1]); if (vR >= vL) "right" else "left" })
  cat(sprintf("gamma = %.1f: V*(1..3) = %s after %d sweeps | policy at 1,2,3: %s\n",
              gamma, paste(round(out$V[2:4], 3), collapse = ", "), out$sweeps, paste(policy, collapse = ", "))) }
## gamma = 0.9: V*(1..3) = 0.81, 0.9, 1 after 4 sweeps | policy at 1,2,3: right, right, right
## gamma = 0.5: V*(1..3) = 0.3, 0.5, 1 after 3 sweeps | policy at 1,2,3: left, right, right

Value iteration reproduces \(V^* = (0.81, 0.9, 1.0)\) for \(\gamma = 0.9\); for \(\gamma = 0.5\) the agent at position 1 turns left. But it needs the rules of the environment — step — in advance. Q-learning learns a table \(Q(s, a)\) from experience alone, trying actions (exploring at random with probability \(\epsilon\)) and updating

\[Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\,\Big[\, r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \,\Big],\]

where the bracket is the temporal-difference error between expectation and observation and \(\alpha\) is a learning rate as in gradient descent. Watkins and Dayan proved that the table converges to \(Q^*\), with \(V^*(s) = \max_a Q^*(s, a)\).[35]

# Q-learning: the same values learned from experience only, without access to the rules.
set.seed(0); gamma <- 0.9; alpha <- 0.5; epsilon <- 0.3
Q <- matrix(0, 5, 2); V_star <- value_iteration(gamma)$V; errors <- numeric(600)
for (episode in 1:600) { s <- 2                                   # every episode starts in the middle
  for (t in 1:50) {
    a <- if (runif(1) < epsilon) sample(2, 1) else which.max(Q[s + 1, ])   # explore or exploit
    r <- step(s, c(-1, 1)[a]); target <- if (r[[3]]) r[[2]] else r[[2]] + gamma * max(Q[r[[1]] + 1, ])
    Q[s + 1, a] <- Q[s + 1, a] + alpha * (target - Q[s + 1, a]); s <- r[[1]]; if (r[[3]]) break }
  errors[episode] <- max(abs(apply(Q[2:4, ], 1, max) - V_star[2:4])) }
cat("learned Q(s,a) for positions 1..3 [left, right]:\n"); print(round(Q[2:4, ], 3))
## learned Q(s,a) for positions 1..3 [left, right]:
##       [,1] [,2]
## [1,] 0.300 0.81
## [2,] 0.729 0.90
## [3,] 0.810 1.00
cat("V from Q =", round(apply(Q[2:4, ], 1, max), 3), "| value iteration =", round(V_star[2:4], 3), "\n")
## V from Q = 0.81 0.9 1 | value iteration = 0.81 0.9 1
plot(errors, type = "l", col = BLUE, log = "y", xlab = "episode", ylab = "max |V from Q - V*|",
     main = "Q-learning converges to the values from value iteration")

Figure 16. Largest error between the values implied by the Q-table and \(V^*\) over 600 episodes. By trial and error alone the agent discovers the values that value iteration computed from the rules — and therefore the same policy: in every position the “right” entry of the table exceeds the “left” one.

Nothing in the Q-learning chunk knows the rewards or transitions; it calls step and observes. That is the sense in which “reinforcement” names a paradigm: the experience is generated by the learner’s actions, the performance is cumulative reward, the task is a policy. Scale the corridor to a patient’s state in intensive care, the actions to doses and the reward to survival, and you have the “AI Clinician” of Section 3.4[12] — with its difficulties: experience taken from records of what clinicians did, a state never fully observed, and a reward as delayed as feedback gets.

Exercise 5

  1. Set epsilon = 0 in the Q-learning chunk. Does the agent still find the right exit? Explain with the first episodes in mind. (b) Set the left reward to 0.85 with \(\gamma = 0.9\). Which exit should the agent take from positions 1 and 2? Confirm with value iteration.

11. Preview: how we will know a model works

Every experiment above measured a model on unseen data, and Section 8 showed why. Supplement S1 develops the methodology; this section fixes its vocabulary.

Training, validation and test sets. The labelled data are split at random into a training set, on which parameters are fitted; a validation set, on which flexibility knobs (degree, \(\lambda\), tree depth, the threshold of Section 9.5) are chosen by comparing candidates; and a test set, touched once at the end to report the performance of the final model on data that influenced none of its decisions. Usual proportions are 60/20/20, 70/15/15 and 80/10/10 per cent, stratified to keep class proportions. With few data, k-fold cross-validation replaces the validation set: divide the training data into \(k\) folds (5 or 10), fit \(k\) times on \(k - 1\) folds, evaluate on the remaining one, average; stratified k-fold keeps class proportions, leave-one-out is \(k = n\).

Overfitting is a model that has learned the accidents of its sample — noise, outliers, spurious correlations — besides the pattern: low training error, high error on new data, as for the degree-15 polynomial; it grows with flexibility, fewer cases and noisier labels, and is detected only on unseen data. Underfitting is a model too rigid for the pattern, with high error on both, as for the line fitted to the sine. The bias–variance decomposition of Supplement S1 explains why generalisation error is U-shaped between them.

Metrics for a classifier. The confusion matrix (Figure 14) tabulates true against predicted classes; for two classes its cells are true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN), true negatives (TN). Accuracy = (TP + TN)/n, misleading with imbalanced classes; precision = TP/(TP + FP), the fraction of positive calls that are right; recall (sensitivity) = TP/(TP + FN), the fraction of true positives caught; specificity = TN/(TN + FP); F1, the harmonic mean of precision and recall; AUC-ROC, the area under the curve of sensitivity against 1 − specificity as the threshold moves (the two curves of Figure 13 plotted against each other), measuring how well the model ranks cases independently of any threshold — 0.5 for a coin, 1.0 for a perfect ranking. For regression the analogues are MSE, RMSE and \(R^2\) on held-out data. Imbalanced classes, thresholds, calibration, confidence intervals and information leakage between splits are developed in Supplement S1, to be read before Unit 3.

12. Summary

You should now be able to explain, without notes:

  • Mitchell’s \(T\), \(P\), \(E\); learning as induction and what that implies about certainty.
  • The seven steps of a data-science project and why machine learning is one of them.
  • Model, loss, optimiser; the paradigms by their feedback (supervised, unsupervised with its four sub-types, reinforcement, semi- and self-supervised); class versus target.
  • The statistical, neural and evolutionary approaches as searches of one hypothesis space; classifier and decision boundary; why k-means is not a classifier.
  • Least squares, the normal equations \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\), the four-point fit by hand, coefficients, \(R^2\), residuals.
  • Gradient descent: update, learning-rate regimes, conditioning and scaling, stochastic variants.
  • Overfitting, underfitting and what ridge adds to the normal equations.
  • Logistic regression: sigmoid, log-odds, log-loss, one probability by hand, threshold as a decision.
  • What k-means, value iteration and Q-learning compute and from what experience.
  • Training/validation/test, cross-validation, confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC.

13. Self-assessment

  1. A hospital wants to flag, at admission, patients likely to need intensive care within 48 hours from their first vital signs and laboratory results. Identify \(T\), \(P\) and \(E\) and the paradigm.
\(T\): assign “ICU within 48 h” or not to an admission from its initial measurements; \(P\): e.g. sensitivity at a fixed false-alarm rate; \(E\): past admissions with outcome. Supervised classification.
  1. Inductive or deductive: (a) “The dosing calculator applies the weight-based rule to this patient”; (b) “In 2,000 past patients this dose was toxic when creatinine clearance was below 30 mL/min, so the rule should include a renal adjustment”?
  1. Deduction: a known rule applied to a case. (b) Induction: a general rule proposed from cases, possibly wrong for cases unlike those observed.
  1. “The data are already in the database, so we can start fitting models tomorrow.” Which steps of the protocol are skipped, and what could go wrong in each?
Problem identification (undefined target: the wrong question answered), cleaning (missing values coded as zeros, duplicated patients, identifiers as features) and exploration (a feature that is a proxy for the label, typing errors as extreme values).
  1. In Figure 3 two methods produced similar lines, and LDA a third close to them. Are the three approaches therefore equivalent?
No. They shared the hypothesis space (lines), so none could find anything else; they differ in how they search, in what else they provide and, with richer spaces, in what they can represent.
  1. Fit a least-squares line by hand to \((1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 6)\).
\(\bar{x} = 2.5\), \(\bar{y} = 4\). Products of deviations: \(3 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 3 = 7\); \(\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 5\). Slope \(1.4\), intercept \(4 - 1.4 \times 2.5 = 0.5\): \(\hat{y} = 0.5 + 1.4x\); residuals \(0.1, -0.3, 0.3, -0.1\), summing to zero.
  1. The rooms coefficient was 9.1 alone and 3.8 with thirteen features. Which is “the effect of rooms”?
Neither, causally. The first is the average difference per room; the second the difference among tracts equal on the other twelve variables, which absorb part of the association.
  1. Gradient descent diverged at rate 0.021 and converged at 0.015. What sets the boundary, and what change to the data moves it to 1.0?
The largest Hessian eigenvalue, \(\lambda_{\max} \approx 102\): convergence needs \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max} \approx 0.0196\). Standardising the feature makes the Hessian of the MSE \(2\mathbf{I}\), so the boundary becomes \(\eta < 1\).
  1. In Figure 9 degree 15 has the lowest training and the highest test error. Explain both, and what ridge changed in Figure 10.
Sixteen parameters pass close to twenty points (small training error); between them the curve follows noise (large test error). Ridge added \(\lambda\mathbf{I}\) to \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\), shrinking the coefficients by orders of magnitude and forcing a smooth curve.
  1. With \(z = 7.32 - 0.63\,t - 1.23\,s\) (thickness \(t\), size \(s\)), compute \(P(\text{benign})\) for thickness 6 and size 2, and the odds ratio per unit of \(s\).
\(z = 7.32 - 3.78 - 2.46 = 1.08\); \(P = 1/(1 + e^{-1.08}) \approx 0.746\), so \(P(\text{malignant}) \approx 0.254\). Odds ratio \(e^{-1.23} \approx 0.29\) per unit of cell size.
  1. Why did the optimal threshold in Figure 13 fall far below 0.5 under a 10 : 1 cost ratio, and what is the cost-optimal threshold in general?
Lowering the threshold converts expensive false negatives into cheap false positives. Calling a case malignant is cheaper in expectation whenever \(P(\text{malignant}) > c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})\); for 10 : 1, \(1/11 \approx 0.09\) (the empirical minimum on the test set was about 0.05).
  1. k-means agreed with the biopsy for 93 % of aspirates without labels. A colleague concludes the labels were unnecessary. What is wrong?
The agreement could only be measured because labels existed; without them nothing says the clusters mean diagnosis rather than size. k-means was also told \(k = 2\), and the supervised methods were at least as good with a probability attached.
  1. In the corridor with \(\gamma = 0.9\), compute \(V(1)\) if the right exit paid 0.5 instead of 1.0, and the policy at position 1.
\(V(3) = 0.5\), \(V(2) = 0.45\), \(V(1) = \max(0.3, 0.405) = 0.405\): still right, barely; with \(\gamma = 0.75\), \(0.28 < 0.3\) and it turns left.

Glossary

Classifier / decision boundary
A function from feature vectors to class labels / the surface where the predicted class changes.
Coefficient of determination (R²)
\(1 - \text{RSS}/\text{TSS}\): the fraction of target variance accounted for by the model.
Cross-validation (k-fold)
Fitting \(k\) times, each holding out one of \(k\) folds, and averaging the scores.
Curse of dimensionality
Degradation of performance as features are added at fixed sample size, because data become sparse.
Deductive / inductive inference
From rules to cases (certain, rigid) / from cases to a rule (probable, generalising); learning is inductive.
Discount factor (γ)
The factor by which a reward one step in the future is devalued relative to an immediate one.
Gradient descent
\(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\nabla L(\theta)\); stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a mini-batch.
IC50 / pIC50
Concentration inhibiting a target’s activity by half / its negative decimal logarithm in mol/L, the usual QSAR target.
Learning rate (η)
The step size of gradient descent; too small is slow, too large diverges.
Least squares / normal equations
Minimising the sum of squared residuals / the linear system \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\) that solves it.
Log-loss (cross-entropy)
The negative mean log-probability assigned to the observed labels; the loss of logistic regression and of neural classifiers.
Logistic regression
\(P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta)\) fitted by maximum likelihood; coefficients are log-odds ratios.
Overfitting / underfitting
Fitting the noise of the sample (low training, high test error) / being too rigid for the pattern (high error on both).
Policy / value function
A mapping from states to actions / the expected discounted cumulative reward from a state.
Regression / classification
Supervised learning with a continuous target / with a categorical target (class, label).
Regularisation (ridge)
A penalty on parameter size added to the loss; ridge uses \(\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2\), i.e. \(\lambda\mathbf{I}\) in the normal equations.
Sigmoid / softmax
\(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\), mapping a score to a probability (inverse: logit) / its \(K\)-class generalisation.
Structured / unstructured data
Data with a predefined model (tables) / without one (text, images, signals), converted by feature extraction.
Supervised / unsupervised / reinforcement learning
Learning from labelled pairs / from inputs alone / from rewards obtained by acting.
Training / validation / test set
Data used to fit parameters / to choose flexibility settings / to report final performance once.

Textbooks

  • Mitchell TM. Machine Learning. McGraw-Hill; 1997. — Chapter 1 for the definition of learning; chapters 4 and 13 for gradient descent and reinforcement learning.
  • James G, Witten D, Hastie T, Tibshirani R. An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R. 2nd ed. Springer; 2021. — Chapters 2–4 cover Sections 6–9 with R code; free PDF at statlearning.com.
  • Hastie T, Tibshirani R, Friedman J. The Elements of Statistical Learning. 2nd ed. Springer; 2009. — Chapters 3–4 for linear and logistic regression and ridge; free PDF.
  • Venables WN, Ripley BD. Modern Applied Statistics with S (MASS). 4th ed. Springer; 2002. — the reference for the R modelling functions used here (lda, nnet, multinom).
  • Sutton RS, Barto AG. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction. 2nd ed. MIT Press; 2018. — Chapters 3–4 and 6 for value iteration and Q-learning; free online.
  • Bishop CM. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer; 2006. — Chapter 1 for the polynomial experiment of Section 8 in its original form.

Online resources

  • CRAN task view “Machine Learning & Statistical Learning” — cran.r-project.org/view=MachineLearning.
  • ChEMBL — ebi.ac.uk/chembl; BindingDB — bindingdb.org; DrugBank — go.drugbank.com; Drug Repurposing Hub — clue.io/repurposing.
  • UCI Machine Learning Repository — archive.ics.uci.edu (the original Wisconsin breast-cancer and Boston housing data).
  • Framingham Heart Study risk functions — framinghamheartstudy.org/fhs-risk-functions.
Study material for BGM-411 Inteligencia Artificial (R edition), Universidad Católica del Maule. This page was knitted from the R-Markdown source U2.Rmd; every figure and number was produced by the R code shown, and the notebook runs in Google Colab (R runtime). Last built 18 October 2026.
